samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Rose Marie Snyder was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Rose Marie Snyder
sp.p: My sister Ann, Ann Trusovsky (ph), was an Army nurse in World War II. She passed away in 1997, so she isn't here to tell her own story, but I remember some of it and some of this is my story too, because I used to visit her often when she was stationed in Kentucky, and I was very interested in everything that went on. She was a senior student at Cleveland City Hospital School of Nursing when Pearl Harbor was attacked. Two of our brothers were already in the service prior to Pearl Harbor. Henry had joined the Marines and Frank had joined the Army. Our brother Gabriel waited for the draft because he had just become engaged to his sweetheart and he didn't want to hurry away. Army recruiters came to the nursing school and Ann signed a pledge to join the Army upon her graduation, which wasn't far off, and she was called up a few months after passing her Ohio State exams. Our brothers were a little put out because she automatically became a second lieutenant, as all the nurses did, and they told her not to expect them to salute her if they happened to come home on furlough at the same time together.

I was just 13 years old when the War broke out and all my siblings marched away, even my big sister. Ann had specialized in psychiatric nursing and so she was sent to a psychiatric Army hospital in Kentucky. It was some distance into the countryside of some miles from a small town called Danville. It was a large hospital and it was surrounded by the usual kind of Army camp with barracks and so forth. At this time, in the beginning of the War, the nurses wore white duty uniforms, just like civilian nurses, and their dress uniforms were blue, while the soldiers wore olive drab and khaki. This changed a little later because, my sister explained to me, it became known to the enemy that our military had a ratio of one nurse to "x" amount of soldiers so all the enemy had to do was to count the white uniforms or the blue dress uniforms to figure out how many men there were. So, the nurses' duty uniforms were changed to tan and white striped seersucker material and they were also issued olive drab dress uniforms. The tan and white uniforms, the duty uniforms, looked like khaki from a distance. The navy nurses' duty uniforms also were changed from the white, like civilians, to blue and white seersucker material. The seersucker was more practical, too. It didn't need ironing. And after the war, this striped seersucker became popular for -- for -- civilian wear. Even men's summer suits were made of it. I think there must have been a huge surplus of that. Something else the military did in clothing was they had these all-weather overcoats made with warm zip-out linings and well, zip-out linings had never existed before then and they're still popular today. Ann said the nurses used the zip-out linings for bathrobes, which was a good idea when you need to keep clothing at a minimum.

While Ann was stationed in Kentucky, she became acquainted with a young medic, Quentin Holley, who she soon married. Quentin had been a premed student at Xavier University in Cincinnati and when the War broke out, he put his education on hold and he joined the Army. He was intent on fighting for his country, but because of his premed education he was assigned to the Medical Corps and he was not very satisfied with this so he put in a request very quickly for a transfer to the infantry and that took a while because of Army red tape and it didn't come through until after he and Ann got married. And then Sergeant Quentin Holley was eventually sent overseas and he was killed in action in Germany.

I went to visit Ann in Kentucky as often as I possibly could. I even played hooky from high school one time to go visit her but that was when she was going to be sent overseas and I -- I -- wanted to see her once more before she went into danger. She taught me how to buy a train ticket in Cleveland, change trains in Cincinnati, and get on the old Southern Railway down to Danville and to take a taxi to the Army post. I did that many times while she was stationed there. The trains were full of servicemen and people traveling through, probably to visit them as I was doing. The train cars were so packed there was standing room only, and people sat on their suitcases in the aisles. And I remember seeing sailors sleeping in the luggage racks above the seats. It seemed like everyone in the country was on the move during that war.

Ann's captain was always so kind to me, to let me have a spare room in the nurses' quarters instead of the visitors' barracks, and to have meals in the Officers' Mess, and I became well acquainted with everything and everyone on the post. I was well known as "Lieutenant Holley's little sister," riding Red Cross bicycles around the roads, playing billiards in the Officers' Rec, and having ice cream sundaes in the PX. I -- I -- did all this while Ann was on duty.

In the psychiatric wards the nurses were rotated periodically because some of the wards were more difficult than others and this way the nurses got a -- a -- break. But Ann worked on one of the difficult wards for quite a long time because the doctor in charge requested for her not to be rotated. He preferred to having her stay.

One night, Ann and I took a walk up the country road that led out of the camp. It was a nice summer night and we liked talking and taking long walks. And on the way back we got to the guard's station at the gate. We saw that he was on the phone and he was looking very nervous and he had one of the patients in the kiosk with him. Patient was looking nervous. Ann recognized the patient as one of hers and she went over to talk to him. He had tried to run away. He said he wanted to go home. Ann put her arm around his shoulder and told him in a kind, gentle voice that he wasn't well enough to go home just yet and that he would be taken good care of a while longer and he could go home after that. And he calmed down and he let a couple of medics come and take him back to the hospital. It was the first time I'd seen one of our soldier patients who'd obviously had a hard time in the War.

The last couple of times that I was able to visit Ann in Kentucky, I was surprised at a huge change in the post. Adjacent at -- to -- it had been built another camp and it was separated from -- from -- the regular Army post by -- by -- a fence and there were new large barracks and a tall guard tower with a big searchlight and I found out that this was a prison camp for the German POW soldiers. During the day these prisoners were everywhere on the Army post. I would see them, working. They washed windows, painted walls, kept the grounds clean and mowed the lawns and the tall grasses of the countryside around the perimeter of the post. And they had riding mowers to do this and sometimes they would have races on the riding mowers on -- on -- this perimeter and I would watch them having a lot of fun. They would be yelling and laughing and I noticed that the guard on duty was enjoying watching them as much as I was. Those prisoners had good clothing and good shoes and looked healthy and well-fed. You could tell they slept well and had plenty of rest.

One day two of them were sent to the nurses' quarters without a guard while I was there and their job was to stencil names and information on the luggage of nurses who were being transferred out. Ann told me that none of the prisoners wanted to escape. They were better cared for here than in their army. They had better clothing, better food and they even got paid for working. Ann told me that prisoners were paid a small amount every day for their work but that some of them told her that they were saving this money so that after the war they could come back to the United States and become citizens. You can see they were taking for granted that we were going to win this war.

What a contrast this was, though, to the horrible POW camp that my brother Frank had been taken prisoner to in Germany when -- where-- many of our men died of malnutrition and their wounds and were always at hard labor and extreme winter temperatures. Their warm clothing was taken away from them when they got captured. My brother risked his life in escaping, rather than stay there and die.

Soon after my last visit to her, Ann was transferred to a port of embarkation in Georgia. She would be going overseas. We didn't know where and, of course, she didn't either. There were a lot of rumors in those days about there being spies around this port in Georgia and I'm sure they were true. Ann said she was sharing a large barracks with only about four or five nurses there in Georgia and that one night as they were all sleeping, and she was closest to the entrance, she was awakened suddenly by a man entering in the dark. He stopped just inside the door and he called out in a loud voice, "How many of you in here?" And quickly thinking she called back, "35." And this man left very quickly. Ann checked with officers the next day and she found, as she expected, that no one had been sent to the barracks late at night to take a head count.

The medical personnel that she was with was sent to the Philippines aboard a hospital ship on which there was nothing to do until they reached their destination. The ship would be picking up our recuperating wounded and bringing them back, and probably the personnel who had been working there for quite awhile, and then the personnel that my sister was with would be remaining to work in the hospital there. So there they were on the ship with nothing to do, so out of boredom everyone stayed below deck having card parties and social times. But Ann was one of those nature-loving people who liked those days on the deck. She liked to watch the sea and the sky and so one day, when she was all alone on the deck observing the waves and the clouds, she saw a barrel floating in the water, some distance from the ship. And it would bob toward the ship and then bob a ways back, and then bob closer to the ship and then bob a ways back. And Ann began to try to figure out mathematically how long it would take a barrel at this rate to bump into the hull. It was something to do. A sailor came walking by and he jokingly said as he passed her, "So what do you think you see out there?" And Ann said, "Well, only a barrel." And at that, the sailor jumped to the railing, looked out and quickly raced off running. And in a few moments Ann said she heard sirens and bells and whistles and the ship suddenly changed course. The barrel had been a mine. She said the sailor was commended for saving the ship, but of course, I think my sister did. What if she had been at the card party?

On the ship they had traveled through the Caribbean and through the Panama Canal and on into the South Pacific to the Philippines. And you would have thought that they would have left from the West Coast, but I guess a ship from Georgia would not be expected by spies to be going to the Pacific. The ship would leave them off in the Philippines and pick up recuperating soldiers and personnel and bring them back home. In the Philippines, she was with a MASH unit, not a psychiatric facility. That was in the States. I don't know if they called it a MASH unit back then, but that -- that's -- what it was. The hospital and the nurses' living quarters and all the personnel lived in tents. And they were told to be very careful because there were hills all around them and there were Japanese snipers in the hills. And one day she came out of her tent -- she was going to hang up some laundry to dry -- and there was a river nearby and up the bank came a huge lizard. She said it was almost the size of a cow. And so she went to all the -- the -- nurses who were still in their tents and told them to zip up their tents because there was this huge animal out there -- she didn't know if it was a carnivore or not.
